title: The rotation read a token's expiry in the projection of its locking SELECT, which PostgreSQL can evaluate before the lock is granted, so a token that expired while the rotation waited was still rotated
resolution: The locking SELECT reads only the state; #expiredUnderLock reads expires_at <= clock_timestamp() in its own statement after the lock; the stepped-clock test holds the row until past expiry and expects token-not-pending with no replacement.

title: The workers view copied a worker's host name and the token answers copied a constraint's host name unredacted, so a secret-shaped value in either left in a list that passed the schema
resolution: workerBody and tokenBody pass the host name through redactSecrets; the stored constraint still matches; a route test enrolls a worker and issues, rotates, and lists a token with secret-shaped host names and checks [redacted] in every answer and the secret field kept.

title: The in-memory registry refused only a known hash, so two tokens with one identifier were stored and a rotation could reuse a stored identifier, unlike the unique column in PostgreSQL
resolution: #add refuses a known identifier as conflict before any write; conformance cases add a token with a known identifier and rotate with a replacement whose identifier exists, and check that the original stays pending.

title: The row-lock race polled pg_stat_activity through the lock holder's own transaction, whose activity snapshot can be kept, so the barrier could time out while both writes waited
resolution: racedForTokenRow polls through a separate observer connection outside any transaction, as the expiry test does.

title: The either-order service test reversed only the call order, so the revocation won in both iterations, and the PostgreSQL race accepted either winner; the record's claim of redemption-first coverage was unfounded
resolution: Gated in-memory tests hold one side at the registry so that each of revocation and redemption wins in turn; PostgreSQL races queue the writes under the row lock so that the first waiter wins and assert the winner; the coverage note names these tests.

title: No test proved that a rotation rolls back whole when the write after the replacement's INSERT fails, and no test raced a rotation against a redemption, a revocation, or another rotation
resolution: A trigger raises on the token's UPDATE after the replacement's INSERT; the test expects no replacement and a pending token. Seven row-lock races and gated in-memory tests cover rotation against redemption, revocation, and rotation in both orders, and a redemption between the lookup and the write.

title: The three mutation controls did not stand in for the ten service tests and four conformance cases that the module's fail-before run never loaded
resolution: Negative controls per behavior group, rotation, revoked-token redemption, replacement reporting, TTL, pagination, rotation atomicity, and secret-free diagnostics, each with its mutation and failing tests recorded.

title: Route and composition assertions used the raw answer text or body as their failure message, so a failure, including the leak check itself, would print a token secret
resolution: Fixed messages and boolean comparisons in every assertion that concerns a token answer; a deliberate failure (the rotation answering 200) was captured and holds no secret.

title: The recorded diff statistics did not match the command's output for the recorded range
resolution: The record carries the command output for the final code commit and names the wrong figures and the actual ones for the earlier range.

title: The record called the uncovered service branches dependency defaults; they were the failure paths of insertion, listing, lookup, and expiry conversion
resolution: The note names the failure paths; tests with a failing registry and a clock past the representable expiry cover them and check that no failure names a secret.
